skill.title: Distinguish population and sample; judge generalisation
skill.output: population, sample, how far conclusions generalise

steps.ask: Which group is every adult in the town, and which group is actually chosen?
steps.title: Identify the population and the sample

lines.text: Population: the 4500 adults in the town. Sample: the 90 adults chosen.

steps.ask: How many adults in the town does each person in the sample stand for? Divide to find out.
steps.title: Divide the population by the sample

steps.ask: What must be true of the 90 for their views to say something about all 4500 adults?
steps.title: State the result

lines.text: The sample is 1 in every 50 adults, so conclusions only generalise if these 90 represent the town.

lesson.note: Changed from problem 1: the answer is now a percentage of the population rather than a 1-in-N ratio, so one more step converts a fraction to a percentage. Naming the population and the sample first stays the same.

steps.title: Write the sample as a fraction of the population

steps.ask: How do you turn a fraction of the whole into a percentage?
steps.title: Convert to a percentage

lesson.note: Changed from problem 2: there are no numbers to work out. It is a written argument about what a sample gains and loses, but it still rests on whether the sample represents the population.

steps.ask: What does a sample save compared with asking everyone in the population?
steps.title: Give an advantage of a sample

lines.text: A $\hl{2}{\text{sample}}$ is cheaper and faster than surveying everyone in the $\hl{1}{\text{population}}$.

steps.ask: What could go wrong with the answers if the sample does not look like the whole population?
steps.title: Give a disadvantage of a sample

lines.text: A $\hl{2}{\text{sample}}$ is less accurate, and it may be biased if it does not represent the whole $\hl{1}{\text{population}}$.

lesson.final: \text{Advantage: cheaper or faster. Disadvantage: less accurate (sampling bias).}

steps.ask: What is the distance from the centre of the interval to its upper limit?

lines.text: The interval is centred on $\hat{p} = 0.35$ and its upper limit is $0.435$.

steps.ask: Which expression do you need for the standard error, and what is it when $\hat{p} = 0.35$?
steps.title: Find p-hat times (1 - p-hat)

steps.ask: How are the margin of error and the standard error linked by the z-value $1.96$?
steps.title: Set up the margin of error equation

steps.ask: How can you remove the square root from the left-hand side?
steps.title: Solve for n

lesson.note: Same goal as Problem 1, finding the sample size for a given margin. It changes from solving one equation with a known p-hat to comparing two margins with a ratio, and the margin is halved from 0.06 to 0.03.

steps.ask: Which part of the margin of error formula changes when $n$ changes, and which part stays the same?
steps.title: Write the margin of error using n

lines.text: Let $k = 1.96\sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}$. It does not change, so the margin of error is $\frac{k}{\sqrt{n}}$.

steps.ask: Write one equation for each margin. Which quantity is different between the two surveys?
steps.title: Write the two margins

steps.ask: If you divide one margin equation by the other, what happens to $k$, and what is left?
steps.title: Divide the second by the first

steps.title: Solve for n

lines.text: Halving the margin of error needs 4 times the sample size.

lesson.note: Changes from calculating n to judging four statements about how the standard error responds to the sample size and p-hat. No numbers are calculated, so the method is different; it is the only other candidate for this skill.

steps.ask: A higher confidence level changes which $z$-value is used. What does a bigger $z$-value do to the margin of error?
steps.title: Statement 1: Always true

lines.text: A higher confidence level needs a larger $z$-value, so the margin of error, and the interval, gets wider.

steps.ask: Does $\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})$ always go up or always go down as $\hat{p}$ changes? Try $\hat{p} = 0$, $0.5$ and $1$.
steps.title: Statement 2: Sometimes true

lines.text: $\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})$ increases as $\hat{p}$ rises towards $0.5$ and then decreases, so the standard error does not always increase.

steps.ask: With $n$ fixed, what happens to the standard error when $\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})$ rises?
steps.title: Statement 3: Always true

lines.text: With $\hl{1}{n}$ fixed, the standard error is the square root of $\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})$ divided by $\hl{1}{n}$, so it rises whenever $\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})$ rises.

steps.ask: What happens to a fraction when its denominator gets bigger?
steps.title: Statement 4: Never true

lines.text: Increasing $\hl{1}{n}$ makes $\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{\hl{1}{n}}$ smaller, so the standard error always decreases.
